Adulterous
a-DUL-ter-us
adj.
From adultery, Latin adulterium, from adulterare, to corrupt or falsify. Webster 1828: guilty of adultery; pertaining to adultery. Scripture uses it chiefly in the spiritual sense — a covenant people unfaithful to the God they are married to.

Biblical Definition

Adulterous in the Gospels is the Lord’s word for a generation, not for an individual, and it draws on the prophets’ picture of Israel as a wife. Twice He uses it in refusing a sign: An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas (Matthew 12:39), and again, A wicked and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign… And he left them, and departed (Matthew 16:4). The demand for a sign is itself named as unfaithfulness — the request of a people who will not trust the Husband they have. He uses it of the setting in which His disciples must own Him: Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels (Mark 8:38). And James applies the same charge to the church, in the sharpest address in the epistles: Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God (James 4:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ADULTEROUS as guilty of adultery; pertaining to adultery; and, in Scripture, idolatrous or apostate — unfaithful to the covenant God as a wife is unfaithful to a husband.

expand to see more

ADULTEROUS, a. — Guilty of adultery; pertaining to adultery.

In Scripture, idolatrous, very wicked, apostate — the covenant relation being figured as a marriage.

ADULTERY, n. — Violation of the marriage bed; a crime against the seventh commandment.

Also, in the Old Testament, the departure of a covenant people from the LORD to other gods.

From Latin adulterare, to corrupt or falsify — the root also of adulterate.

Key Scripture

Matthew 12:39 — "But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas:"

Matthew 16:4 — "A wicked and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given unto it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas. And he left them, and departed."

Mark 8:38 — "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."

James 4:4 — "Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God."

Modern Corruption

James 4:4 states that friendship with the world is enmity with God, which the long evangelical project of cultural relevance has effectively reversed into a strategy.

expand to see more

James writes to Christians, calls them adulterers and adulteresses, and puts the matter as a question they should already be able to answer: know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? The word for world here is not the created order and not the people God loves in John 3:16; it is the organised system of human life arranged without reference to Him. What James forbids is not engagement with unbelievers — the Lord was called a friend of publicans and sinners — but the courting of the world’s approval, values and methods by people already married to God. The seeker-oriented reconstruction of worship, the pursuit of cultural credibility, and the anxiety that the church should not appear strange are all attempts at exactly the friendship James calls enmity, and the harder the church has worked at it the fewer converts it has made.

Matthew 12:39 explains why the demand for signs is a mark of unfaithfulness rather than of open-mindedness. Christ had just healed a man with a withered hand and cast out a devil, and the Pharisees asked for a sign; the request was not for evidence but for a performance on their terms. His answer gives them one sign only — Jonah, three days and three nights, that is, His death and resurrection — which is the sign He has given ever since and the one the church proclaims. Mark 8:38 supplies the personal application, and it is the sharpest word in the Gospels about respectability: to be ashamed of Christ and His words in an adulterous generation is to be met with His shame in the glory of the Father.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek moichalis (G3428), an adulteress, and adjectivally adulterous; moicheia (G3430), adultery; philia (G5373), friendship; Hebrew naaph (H5003), to commit adultery, used of idolatry.

expand to see more

Greek moichalis (G3428) — an adulteress; used adjectivally of the generation (Matthew 12:39; Mark 8:38).

Greek moicheia (G3430) — adultery; the seventh commandment’s subject in the New Testament.

Greek philia (G5373) — friendship, affection; the friendship of the world (James 4:4).

Hebrew naaph (H5003) — to commit adultery; used throughout Jeremiah and Ezekiel of Israel’s idolatry.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to go a-whoring; the prophets’ harsher term for the same unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:2).

Usage

"An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign (Matthew 12:39) — the demand for a sign named as unfaithfulness."

"Ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation (Mark 8:38) — the sharpest word about respectability."

"The friendship of the world is enmity with God (James 4:4) — addressed to Christians, as a question they should be able to answer."
